notes.title: Buy reliability with fewer steps or with verification gates

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
Cutting steps reduces what the agent can do. Isn't that just scope reduction?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
When would you gate rather than cut, even though cutting is cheaper?
Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling
Your gate's retry doubles work on the gated step. At scale, does that stay worth it?
Tier 4 — Open-ended design
Design a reliability programme for an agent currently at 60% task success.
⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Consistency across runs as the reliability target, not best-of-k — Measuring agent reliability: pass^k (arXiv 2507.10995)

  • Fewer steps and simpler composition as the first reliability move — Building Effective AI Agents (Anthropic)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • the 95% problem — why per-step accuracy doesn't survive multiplication.

  • reliability problem — the reliability problem in its general form.

  • reliability engineering — the controls available.

What this note adds: the spend decision. Those notes establish that p^N is the problem; this is the fork between the two ways to fix it — reduce N or raise the effective p with gates — and the arithmetic that says which buys more for your run.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The arithmetic? p^N. At 0.95 and ten steps, ≈ 0.60.
The two levers? Cut N, or raise effective p with a deterministic gate.
Which is cheaper? Cutting steps — it lowers cost and latency at the same time.
When gates win? When the step can't be removed and a check exists.
What a gate needs to work? A deterministic check. A critic model doesn't raise p much.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Reliability in an agent is p^N, so there are exactly two moves: make N smaller or make p bigger. Cutting steps is almost always the better buy, because it improves reliability, cost and latency together — and most agents have steps that exist because control flow was handed to the model rather than because the work needs them. Verification gates raise effective p on the steps you can't remove, but only when the check is deterministic; a critic model shares the generator's blind spots and moves the number far less than people expect. So: cut first, gate what's left.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Cut steps Steps exist that are enumerable or deterministic. Almost always first. Less adaptivity; some scope moves to code. Step count varies wildly on similar inputs.
Deterministic gate A step can't be removed and a real check exists. Verification time per step; a retry path. Tests, schema, execution, citation resolution available.
Critic gate No deterministic check and you need some signal. ~2× per gated step for a correlated opinion. Free-text output where "better" is judgement.
Accept and escalate Neither lever is available and stakes are high. Human minutes; an escalation queue. Judgement output, consequential, no verifier.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Cut steps Deterministic code replaces model steps; often a workflow shape. Improves all three: reliability, cost, latency. Fewer moving parts; failures name a function.
Deterministic gate A checker in the loop plus a bounded retry. Verification cost per step; retries are productive. Gate pass-rate is a live quality signal.
Critic gate A second model call per gated step. ~2× on that step, unverifiable gain. Hard to tell it's helping without a separate eval.
Escalate A confidence signal and a human path. Cost moves to human minutes. Escalation rate becomes the headline metric.

The redraw test: cutting steps makes the diagram smaller; gating adds a checker box with a loop back. If a reliability plan changes neither, it's a prompt change hoping for a different outcome.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The base arithmetic. With per-step success p over N steps:

p^N        0.95^10 ≈ 0.60      0.95^5  ≈ 0.77
           0.97^10 ≈ 0.74      0.97^5  ≈ 0.86

Halving the step count from ten to five at p = 0.95 moves end-to-end from 0.60 to 0.77 — seventeen points, bought by removing work rather than by improving anything.

What a gate is worth. A deterministic gate with a retry turns one attempt into two on the gated step, so effective per-step success goes from p to 1 − (1−p)². At p = 0.95 that's 0.9975 for that step. Gating three of ten steps at 0.95 moves the run from 0.95^10 ≈ 0.60 to roughly 0.95^7 × 0.9975^3 ≈ 0.69. Real, but less than halving the steps — and it costs verification time on every pass.

Why the critic version underperforms. The retry arithmetic above assumes the check is right. A model critic agrees with the generator on the cases they're both wrong about, so the second attempt isn't independent and the effective gain is a fraction of 1 − (1−p)². That's why the order is deterministic checks first, critic last — and why "add a reviewer step" so often produces flat eval scores.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["📉 End-to-end success too low"] --> B["🔢 Count steps in a real trace"]
    B --> C{"🔀 Any step deterministic<br/>or enumerable?"}
    C -->|"yes"| D(["✂️ Move it to code — cut N"])
    C -->|"no"| E{"🔀 Does a real check<br/>exist for a step?"}
    E -->|"yes"| F(["🛡️ Deterministic gate + bounded retry"])
    E -->|"no"| G{"🔀 Are the stakes<br/>high?"}
    G -->|"yes"| H(["🙋 Confidence + escalate"])
    G -->|"no"| I(["📝 Critic gate — measure whether it helps"])

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#60A5FA,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style C fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style E fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style G fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style D fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style F fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style H fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style I fill:#FCA5A5,stroke:#F87171,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

The first action is counting, not designing. Most teams don't know their step-count distribution, and it's the input to every branch below — you cannot decide between cutting and gating without knowing how many steps there are and which ones are doing real work.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We added a validation step after every model call and success only went up four points."

Root cause. The team read the compounding argument and responded by gating everything, but the gates were schema checks — they verified that each step's output was well-formed, which it nearly always was. The actual failures were semantic: correct-looking outputs that were wrong about the task. Gating raised p against a failure mode that wasn't happening while adding latency to every step, and the step count — eighteen, on a task that needed about six — went untouched.

Fix. Counting the trace first. Eleven of the eighteen steps were the agent re-deriving things it could have looked up or had already computed, and collapsing those into three task-level tools took the run to seven steps. That alone moved end-to-end success more than the gates had, at lower cost and latency. The gates stayed on the two steps where a real check existed — an executable query and a citation resolution — and were removed elsewhere.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Cutting steps reduces what the agent can do. Isn't that just scope reduction?

Sometimes, and when it is I'd say so. But most of the steps I'd cut aren't capability — they're the model rediscovering structure that was already known. An agent that takes four steps to work out which API to call, when the routing could be a function, is spending reliability on something that has a right answer.

The test is whether the step involves judgement. If it does, cutting it is scope reduction and I'd weigh it honestly. If it doesn't, cutting it is free reliability, and those are usually the majority.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

When would you gate rather than cut, even though cutting is cheaper?

When the step is irreducibly judgement and a real check exists for its output. Code generation is the clean case: you can't remove the step, and tests give you a deterministic verdict, so a gate with a bounded retry turns roughly p into 1 − (1−p)² for real.

The other case is where a step's failure is expensive rather than frequent. A low-probability failure on an irreversible action is worth gating even though the arithmetic barely moves, because the metric that matters there isn't end-to-end success — it's the cost of the tail.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Your gate's retry doubles work on the gated step. At scale, does that stay worth it?

It depends on the gate's pass rate, which is why I'd measure it rather than assume. A gate passing 99% of the time costs the verification on every call and buys almost nothing — the retry path barely fires — so at scale that's pure latency and I'd remove it or sample it.

A gate passing 80% is doing real work and the retry is productive. The number to watch is verification cost against the change in end-to-end success, evaluated per gate rather than in aggregate, because gates are usually not equally valuable and teams tend to add them uniformly. The other scaling consideration is that retries interact badly with rate limits: a gate that fires often under load turns into extra concurrent calls at exactly the wrong moment.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design a reliability programme for an agent currently at 60% task success.

First I'd classify, not optimise. Sample fifty failures and bucket them by earliest fault — planning, tool, context, model — because the response differs entirely and spending before classifying is how teams end up with eighteen gates.

Then the order: cut steps the classification says are unproductive, fix tool contracts and error strings where the tool bucket is large, and only then add gates on the steps that remain and have real checks. I'd keep step count as the headline engineering metric because it's the one that moves cost, latency and reliability together, and it's measurable from traces I already have.

What I'd set up alongside is the measurement to know whether any of it worked: a fixed eval set run in CI on every prompt, tool or graph change, reporting pass^k rather than a single-run score. Without that, improvements are anecdotes and regressions are invisible until a user finds them.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Our steps are 97% accurate, so the agent is reliable."

✅ Reality: Per-step accuracy compounds. At 0.97 over fifteen steps you're at about 0.63 end to end. Step accuracy is a debugging metric; the number you commit to is end-to-end task success.

❌ Trap: "Add a verification step after every model call."

✅ Reality: A gate only helps if its check is real and the failure mode it catches is the one occurring. Schema gates on a semantic failure add latency and change nothing. Measure each gate's pass rate and its effect on end-to-end success separately.

❌ Trap: "A reviewer model is a verification gate."

✅ Reality: It's a correlated second opinion. The retry arithmetic assumes an independent check; a critic sharing the generator's context and blind spots delivers a fraction of it. Deterministic checks first, critic last, and only when nothing else exists.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • the 95% problem — the compounding this note spends against.

  • reliability engineering — the control surface.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §1 Which rung of the ladder — cutting steps often means demoting a rung.

  • §8 Verification gates — this note decides where they go.

  • §4 Tool granularity — collapsing steps into task-level tools is the main way N falls.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 "Our agent succeeds 60% and costs too much" — this note is the method for that problem.

  • §14 Coding agent — tests make the gate branch unambiguously correct there.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Spend and rate limits enforced outside the model — OWASP LLM10: Unbounded Consumption

  • Wall-clock and step limits as run-level controls — LangGraph: durable execution

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • spend and rate limits — spend caps and where they're enforced.

  • reliability engineering — budgets among the reliability controls.

What this note adds: that you need all four and they aren't interchangeable, plus the part usually left undesigned — a cap is a branch, not an exception, so each one needs a defined behaviour on trip.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The four? Steps · tokens · wall-clock · loop detection on repeated calls.
Why all four? Each catches a different runaway; a run finds whichever you left open.
What a cap must have? A defined behaviour on trip — partial answer, escalate, or fail.
Where the spend cap lives? The gateway. Outside the thing being capped.
The cheapest detector? Identical tool call with identical arguments, twice.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I set four caps because they catch different runaways. A step cap catches a loop that keeps deciding to continue. A token cap catches a single step dragging a huge context. A wall-clock cap catches a tool that hangs. And loop detection — the same call with the same arguments twice — catches the agent that's stuck without exceeding anything. The part usually missing is what happens on trip: a cap that raises an exception produces a failed run and a confused user, so each one needs a defined branch, normally return what you have and say what's missing.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Step cap only Simple agents, short runs. Misses hangs and context blow-ups. One tool, fast, bounded output.
All four caps Anything in production. The default. Four values to tune per agent. Runs vary in shape; tools call other systems.
Caps with graceful branches Users are waiting and a partial answer has value. Designing the partial-answer path. "Tell me what you found so far."
Caps as hard failures Batch work where partial output is meaningless. A user-visible failure on every trip. Correctness is all-or-nothing.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you set Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Step cap A counter in the loop with a named terminal state. Bounds worst-case tokens indirectly. Cap-trip rate says whether the shape fits the task.
Token cap Per-step and per-run accounting against the model call. Bounds cost directly — the one that maps to money. Token-per-run distribution; the tail is your bill.
Wall-clock A deadline propagated into tool calls, not just the loop. Bounds latency, which is often the SLA. Timeout rate per tool identifies the slow dependency.
Loop detection Hash of tool name plus arguments, compared across steps. Catches waste the other three would let run to the cap. Repeat rate is the earliest signal of a stuck agent.

The redraw test: caps live in the harness and the gateway, and each needs a labelled exit from the loop. If the diagram's loop has one exit marked "done", the cap behaviour hasn't been designed.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why the step cap doesn't bound cost on its own. Cost grows with accumulated context, so a twelve-step cap on a run carrying a large document is a much bigger bill than the same cap on a lean run. The token cap is the one that maps to money; the step cap maps to reliability, since it bounds the exponent in p^N.

Setting the step cap honestly. Take the step-count distribution from real traces and put the cap above p99, not at the mean. A cap at the median converts normal long runs into failures, and teams then raise it reactively until it stops firing — at which point it isn't a control. Cap above the legitimate tail and treat trips as a signal that something is wrong rather than as routine.

Loop detection, which is nearly free. Hash tool name plus normalised arguments per step and compare. A repeat is strong evidence the agent has lost track — it's not receiving new information and is choosing the same action, which is the shape of a stuck run. It fires long before a step cap would, and it catches the case where the agent alternates between two calls indefinitely, which a naive "same as last step" check misses.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["🔁 Step completes"] --> B{"🔀 Same call as a<br/>previous step?"}
    B -->|"yes"| C(["🔄 Loop detected — break with what you have"])
    B -->|"no"| D{"🔀 Step cap reached?"}
    D -->|"yes"| E(["✋ Return partial + say what's missing"])
    D -->|"no"| F{"🔀 Token or wall-clock<br/>budget exhausted?"}
    F -->|"yes"| E
    F -->|"no"| G(["▶️ Continue"])

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style D fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style F fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style C fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style E fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style G fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

Both trip paths land in the same place deliberately: return what exists and name the gap. An agent that says "I checked three of five sources and ran out of budget" is useful; one that raises a timeout after ninety seconds is not, and they cost the same to produce.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "A single run cost forty dollars. We had a step cap."

Root cause. The step cap was twenty and the run used nineteen, so nothing tripped. What made it expensive was that step four had pulled a large document into context and nothing removed it, so every subsequent step re-billed it — the run was within its step budget and vastly outside any sane token budget, which didn't exist. The step cap had been treated as the budget because it's the one frameworks expose most prominently, and it bounds the wrong quantity.

Fix. A per-run token cap enforced at the gateway with a per-tenant daily ceiling above it, plus offloading the document to a reference. The distinction worth carrying: the step cap bounds reliability, the token cap bounds cost, and a system with only one of them is unbounded in the other dimension.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Where do these caps actually live?

Steps, wall-clock and loop detection live in the harness, because they're properties of one run and the loop is what enforces them. The spend cap lives in the gateway, outside the run — that's the only position that survives a runaway loop, since anything inside the thing being capped depends on the thing being capped behaving.

The per-tenant ceiling also sits at the gateway, above the per-run cap, so one customer's many runs can't aggregate into a bill nobody authorised even when each individual run is well-behaved.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

A partial answer on a cap trip sounds nice, but isn't a wrong partial answer worse than none?

It can be, and the distinction is whether the partial result is labelled. An answer that says which sources it checked and which it didn't lets the reader judge it; an answer that silently omits half the ground looks complete and is worse than a failure.

So the branch isn't just "return what you have" — it's "return what you have, with the gap stated". Where the output feeds an automated consumer rather than a person, I'd fail instead, because a downstream system can't read the caveat and will treat partial as complete.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Cap trips are rare individually. At scale, what do they tell you?

The rate is a design signal rather than an incident stream. A step-cap trip rate that's stable and low means the cap is doing its job on genuine outliers. A rate that's rising means either the task distribution shifted — harder questions arriving — or something regressed in the harness, and both want investigating before users notice.

What I'd watch specifically is trips by cap type, because they point at different problems. Rising step trips suggest the shape is wrong for newly arriving inputs; rising wall-clock trips usually mean a dependency got slower; rising loop detections are nearly always a tool whose error message stopped being actionable. That last correlation is the most useful one in practice, because it's the cheapest thing to fix.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design budgets for a platform where tenants buy different tiers.

Budgets become a policy object attached to the tenant rather than constants in the harness: per-run step, token and wall-clock caps, plus a per-tenant daily spend ceiling, all resolved at the gateway when a run is admitted. The harness receives its caps as run parameters, so there's one place the policy lives and the agent code doesn't know about tiers.

Degradation is where the tiers should actually differ. Rather than a lower tier failing sooner, it should do less — fewer sub-agents, a cheaper model for non-critical steps, narrower retrieval. That way the product difference is breadth rather than reliability, which is a much easier thing to sell and to explain when someone hits their limit.

The metric I'd expose to tenants is consumption against ceiling, not just usage, because the support conversation you want is "you're at 80% of your daily budget" before the one that starts with a failed run.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "The step cap is our budget."

✅ Reality: It bounds the exponent in p^N, not the bill. A run inside its step budget can carry a large context and cost many times a normal run. Step cap for reliability, token cap for cost — you need both.

❌ Trap: "We'll put the spend limit in the system prompt."

✅ Reality: A prompt is a request to the component you're trying to constrain, and it's precisely the component that's malfunctioning when the cap matters. Enforce at the gateway, where the counter is checked before dispatch.

❌ Trap: "Hitting a cap is an error, so raise an exception."

✅ Reality: A cap is a branch. The run has done real work and should return it with the gap named. An exception discards the work, tells the user nothing useful, and costs exactly the same to produce.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • spend and rate limits — the spend half.

  • reliability engineering — budgets among the controls.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §8 Fewer steps or more gates — the step cap is where the N conversation gets a number.

  • §10 Spend caps per run and per tenant — the gateway half of this decision.

  • §7 Cancellation & timeouts — the wall-clock cap uses the same propagation path.

  • §2 The layers — the gateway exists partly so these caps have somewhere to live.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 "Our agent succeeds 60% and costs too much" — the missing token cap is usually part of the answer.

  • §14 Deep research agent — step and cost caps are what make unbounded search safe to ship.

notes.title: What is safe to retry, and at which layer

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
Why does the tool layer own retries rather than the HTTP client?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
When is letting the agent retry actually better than retrying in code?
Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling
At high concurrency, what does retry behaviour do to your rate limits?
Tier 4 — Open-ended design
Design retry policy for a platform where teams register their own tools.
⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Exponential backoff with jitter, and why jitter is not optional — Exponential backoff and jitter (AWS Architecture Blog)

  • Idempotency keys, which decide whether a retry is safe at all — Stripe API: idempotent requests

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Tool error handling — classify the failure, retry only transient, don't retry non-idempotent writes.

  • reliability engineering — retries among the controls.

What this note adds: the layering. An agent has three places a retry can live — the HTTP client, the tool layer, and the agent loop itself — and they compose multiplicatively. Nobody designs that on purpose, which is how a transient blip becomes thirty calls.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The three retry layers? HTTP client · tool layer · the agent loop deciding to try again.
Why that's dangerous? They multiply. 3 × 3 × a looping agent is a storm.
What makes a retry safe? Idempotency key — and a classification saying the failure is transient.
Why jitter? Without it, backoff synchronises every client into the same retry wave.
The agent-specific layer? The model retrying by choosing to call again. Budget-bounded, not code-bounded.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

The retry rules are the ordinary ones — classify the failure, retry only transient, exponential backoff with jitter, never retry a non-idempotent write without a key. What's specific to agents is that there's a third retry layer nobody accounts for: the model can decide to call the tool again. That retry isn't bounded by your retry config, it's bounded by the step budget, so an HTTP client retrying three times inside a tool layer retrying three times inside an agent that tries five times is forty-five calls from one blip. I pick one layer to own retries and make the others pass failures through.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
HTTP client only Transient network faults; tools are thin wrappers. The agent can't distinguish "retried and failed" from "failed". Tools are single API calls.
Tool layer owns retries The default — one place with idempotency and classification. Tool code carries the policy; must be consistent across tools. Tools compose several calls.
Let the agent retry The failure needs a different approach, not the same call again. Unbounded by config; consumes step budget. Errors that say what to change.
No retries, fail fast Writes without idempotency keys; anything ambiguous. Transient faults become run failures. Non-idempotent effects you can't make safe.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Client Retry config in the HTTP layer; invisible above it. Cheap; no model calls consumed. Retries hidden from traces unless you instrument them.
Tool layer Classification plus backoff plus key, per tool. Bounded and visible; no step budget consumed. Retry rate per tool is a live dependency-health signal.
Agent retries Nothing structural — it's the loop doing its job. Consumes steps, and re-bills context each attempt. Shows as step-count inflation; needs loop detection to bound.
Fail fast Errors propagate to the agent immediately. Cheapest. Higher visible failure rate — which may be the honest number.

The redraw test: retries are invisible in most diagrams, which is the problem. Drawing which layer owns them is what stops the multiplication, and it's a one-line annotation on the tool-layer box.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The multiplication. Three layers each retrying three times is 3³ = 27 calls from one failure, and if the agent then loops it's bounded only by the step cap. That's the retry storm in miniature — and at scale, every client doing this simultaneously is how a degraded dependency becomes a dead one.

Why jitter matters more than backoff. Exponential backoff alone synchronises clients: everyone fails at once, everyone waits the same interval, everyone retries at once. Jitter spreads the retries across the window, which is the difference between a recovering service and one held down by its own clients. The AWS write-up on this is the canonical reference and the phrasing worth borrowing — full jitter, not fixed backoff.

The agent's own retry, which has no config. When a tool returns an actionable error and the model tries again with corrected arguments, that's a retry — but it's a productive one, because the second attempt differs. When the error isn't actionable the model retries with the same or near-same arguments, which is unproductive and bounded only by the step budget. So tool error quality is what determines whether the agent's retry layer is useful or wasteful, which is the same lever as §2's harness argument.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["❌ A tool call fails"] --> B{"🔀 Transient?<br/>5xx, timeout, 429"}
    B -->|"no — 4xx, validation"| C(["📨 Return an actionable error;<br/>let the agent correct"])
    B -->|"yes"| D{"🔀 Does it have<br/>an idempotency key?"}
    D -->|"no, and it writes"| E(["🛑 Fail fast — don't risk a duplicate"])
    D -->|"yes, or it's a read"| F(["🔁 Retry: backoff + full jitter, bounded"])
    F --> G{"🔀 Still failing after<br/>the bound?"}
    G -->|"yes"| C

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style D fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style G fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style C fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#60A5FA,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style E fill:#FCA5A5,stroke:#F87171,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style F fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

The left branch is the agent-specific part. A 4xx isn't retryable in code but often is correctable by the model — wrong argument, missing field, bad id — so the right move is returning an error good enough for the agent to fix rather than retrying it mechanically or failing the run.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "A two-minute blip at a provider turned into a forty-minute outage for us."

Root cause. Three retry layers nobody had designed together. The HTTP client retried three times with fixed backoff, the tool wrapper caught the resulting failure and retried twice more, and the agent — seeing an unhelpful error — tried the call again itself, several times, within its step budget. One transient failure produced dozens of calls. With every concurrent run doing the same and no jitter anywhere, the retries arrived in synchronised waves, so the provider's recovery window was continuously re-saturated by our own traffic long after the original fault cleared.

Fix. The tool layer became the single retry owner with full jitter and a bound, the HTTP client's retries were disabled, and tool errors were rewritten so the agent could tell "transient, already retried, give up" from "your arguments were wrong, try differently". A circuit breaker per provider went in alongside, which is the next note. The generalisable point: retries are only safe when exactly one layer owns them.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why does the tool layer own retries rather than the HTTP client?

Because the tool layer is the only place that knows both the transport failure and the business semantics. The HTTP client sees a 500 and can't tell whether this endpoint is idempotent; the agent sees an error string and can't do backoff. The tool layer has the idempotency key, the classification and the policy.

It's also the layer where a retry is observable in the right way — one tool call with three attempts, rather than an invisible client retry or a step-budget-consuming agent retry that looks like the agent being indecisive.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

When is letting the agent retry actually better than retrying in code?

When the right response is a different call rather than the same one. A validation error, a not-found on a guessed id, an argument the API rejected — code can only repeat the failing call, while the model can correct it. That's why those errors should come back as messages rather than be retried mechanically.

The condition is error quality. If the message says what was wrong and what a valid call looks like, the agent's retry is productive and usually succeeds in one attempt. If it says "bad request", the agent retries blindly and burns step budget, which is the expensive version of the same mechanism.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

At high concurrency, what does retry behaviour do to your rate limits?

It consumes them at the worst possible moment. Retries arrive when a dependency is already degraded, so you're adding load precisely when there's least capacity — and for model calls specifically, retries count against the same tokens-per-minute budget as real work, so a retry storm reduces useful throughput rather than just adding overhead.

That argues for two things beyond jitter: a circuit breaker so a persistently failing dependency stops receiving retries at all, and a retry budget — a cap on what fraction of calls may be retries, shared across the fleet. The budget is the less common control and the more useful one, because it bounds aggregate behaviour rather than per-client behaviour, and retry storms are an aggregate phenomenon.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design retry policy for a platform where teams register their own tools.

I'd make retries a platform behaviour driven by declaration rather than implementation. A tool declares its direction, whether it's idempotent, and which error codes are transient; the platform applies backoff with jitter, honours the bound, and attaches the idempotency key. Teams don't write retry loops, because that's where the multiplication comes from.

The declaration that matters most is idempotency, and I'd default it to false. A tool that hasn't declared itself idempotent gets fail-fast on writes, which is the safe direction — the alternative default has a team shipping a duplicate-charge bug by omission.

I'd also make the retry budget a platform-level control with per-tenant shares, and expose retry rate per tool so a team can see their dependency degrading before it becomes an incident. That metric only exists because retries happen in one declared place; scattered across three layers it's unmeasurable.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We use exponential backoff, so retries are safe."

✅ Reality: Backoff without jitter synchronises clients into waves that keep a recovering service down. And backoff says nothing about whether the operation is safe to repeat — that's idempotency, a separate property.

❌ Trap: "Retry everything that fails; it's transient more often than not."

✅ Reality: Retrying a 4xx repeats a call that was wrong. Classify first — transient gets a retry, a client error gets an actionable message back to the agent, and a non-idempotent write without a key gets neither.

❌ Trap: "The agent retrying is the agent being robust."

✅ Reality: It's a retry layer with no configuration, bounded only by the step budget. Productive when the error tells it what to change, pure waste when it doesn't — and invisible as a retry unless you're watching for repeated calls.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Tool error handling — classification and the retry rules.

  • HLD reference index §18, §60 — idempotency keys and exactly-once effects.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §8 Circuit breakers — the control that stops retries against a dead dependency.

  • §4 Read tools vs write tools — the write lane is where retry safety is decided.

  • §8 Hard budgets — loop detection is what bounds the agent's own retry layer.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — a retried refund is the failure this prevents.

  • §14 Internal agent platform — declared idempotency is the Tier 4 mechanism.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Circuit breaker — states, thresholds and the half-open probe — Pattern: Circuit Breaker (microservices.io)

  • Model deprecation and version pinning, which is why fallback is a standing requirement — Anthropic: model deprecations

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • reliability engineering — fallback among the reliability controls.

  • HLD reference index — circuit breaker, bulkhead and failover in their general form.

What this note adds: what's different when the dependency is a model. A breaker on a database is about availability; a breaker on a model provider is also about behaviour, because the fallback model is a different component that will answer differently — so failover is a quality event, not just an availability one.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Breaker granularity? Per tool and per provider. One dead tool shouldn't trip everything.
What's different for models? The fallback answers differently — failover changes behaviour, not just uptime.
What must be pinned? The model version. A silent provider update is an untested change.
What trips it? Error rate over a window, not consecutive failures.
The half-open step? One probe request before closing. Never a full reopen.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I put a circuit breaker on each tool and each model provider, because failures aren't global — one dead integration shouldn't stop an agent that could still do most of its job. What's different from a normal breaker is that the model fallback isn't equivalent: a cheaper or different-vendor model will answer differently, so failing over is a quality event and needs its own eval, not just a health check. I pin model versions for the same reason — a silent provider-side update is an untested deploy of my most important dependency.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
No breaker Prototype only. Retries keep hammering a dead dependency; latency collapses. Everything works until something doesn't.
Breaker per tool Multiple integrations with independent failure modes. A breaker's state to manage per tool. One flaky third-party API among several.
Breaker per provider + model fallback Production, always. A second provider to evaluate and keep prompts portable for. Model outages are real and regular.
Degrade instead of failover The fallback's answers aren't good enough to ship. A narrower answer, which you must communicate. Quality gap between primary and fallback is large.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Per-tool breaker State per tool; open trips route to a degraded path. Stops wasting calls on a dead dependency. Breaker state is a dashboard; flapping needs tuning.
Provider failover A second provider integration and prompt portability. Fallback may cost more or less — usually different. Two providers to monitor, and a quality delta to track.
Model fallback (same provider) A model tier ladder with per-tier evals. Cheaper on the fallback path. Success rate per tier — the fallback's quality is a live number.
Degrade A quality knob rather than a substitute. Reduces spend under failure. Users must be told, or trust erodes silently.

The redraw test: breakers are state next to each dependency, and a fallback is a second arrow out of the model router. If the diagram has one model box and one arrow, failover hasn't been designed.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

What trips a breaker. Error rate over a rolling window, not consecutive failures — consecutive-failure counting is fooled by interleaved success from a partially degraded dependency. A workable shape is: open above a failure threshold over a window with a minimum request count, stay open for a cool-down, then half-open and allow a single probe. The minimum-request condition matters because a 100% failure rate on two requests is noise.

Why the half-open probe is one request. Closing the breaker fully after a cool-down sends the entire backlog at a service that may still be unwell, which re-trips it immediately and produces flapping. One probe, then close on success, is the difference between recovery and oscillation.

The model-specific number. Before relying on a fallback, measure task success on the fallback model against the primary on the same eval set. That delta is what failover actually costs you, and it's the number to have when someone asks "can we just fail over?" — if the fallback scores materially worse, failover is a degradation you must communicate, not a transparent recovery.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

flowchart TD
    A["⚠️ A dependency is failing"] --> B{"🔀 Is it a tool<br/>or the model?"}
    B -->|"tool"| C{"🔀 Can the agent work<br/>without it?"}
    B -->|"model"| D{"🔀 Does a fallback<br/>score acceptably?"}
    C -->|"yes"| E(["🔌 Open the breaker; continue degraded"])
    C -->|"no"| F(["🙋 Escalate — the agent can't complete"])
    D -->|"yes"| G(["🔀 Fail over; flag the run as degraded"])
    D -->|"no"| H(["📉 Degrade scope, or queue until recovery"])

    style A fill:#D1D5DB,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style B fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style C fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style D fill:#C4B5FD,stroke:#8B5CF6,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style E fill:#6EE7B7,stroke:#34D399,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style F fill:#FCD34D,stroke:#F59E0B,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style G fill:#93C5FD,stroke:#60A5FA,color:#000000,font-weight:bold
    style H fill:#FCA5A5,stroke:#F87171,color:#000000,font-weight:bold

The branch worth arguing is the one on the right. "Does the fallback score acceptably" is an eval question, not an ops question, and it has to have been answered before the outage — which means the fallback needs to be in your regular eval runs even though it's rarely used.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "We failed over cleanly during the provider outage and then spent two weeks on quality complaints."

Root cause. The fallback was a cheaper model from a second vendor, wired and tested for availability — requests succeeded, latency was fine, no errors. What hadn't been tested was behaviour: the fallback followed the tool schema less reliably, so the agent's tool calls were more often malformed, and its outputs were more verbose in a way that pushed some runs into context pressure. None of that shows on a health check. The outage lasted an hour; the degraded outputs were produced and shipped to customers throughout, and nothing marked those runs as different.

Fix. The fallback joined the regular eval suite with its own scores, and failover began tagging runs as degraded so the outputs were traceable afterwards. A quality gate was added to the failover decision itself — if the fallback's most recent eval score is below a threshold, the breaker routes to degradation or queueing rather than to a worse answer delivered confidently.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why a breaker per tool rather than one for the agent?

Because failures aren't global and the agent usually has partial capability. If the calendar integration is down but search and the database are fine, an agent-level breaker takes everything offline for one dead dependency, when the honest behaviour is to continue and tell the user what it couldn't check.

Per-tool also gives you the diagnostic for free: which breaker is open tells you which dependency is unwell, whereas an agent-level failure tells you only that something is.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Failing over to a different vendor sounds good. What's the real cost of maintaining that?

Prompt and tool-schema portability, mostly. Models differ in how reliably they follow schemas, how they handle system prompts, and how verbose they are, so a prompt tuned for one vendor is not neutral on another. Keeping that portability means avoiding vendor-specific features in the hot path and evaluating both — which is a standing tax, not a one-off.

The question I'd ask to decide whether it's worth paying: what does an hour of unavailability actually cost? For an internal tool, queueing through an outage is fine and a second vendor is over-engineering. For a customer-facing product with an SLA, the tax is cheap insurance.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

The breaker flaps — opening and closing repeatedly. What's wrong?

Usually the threshold is measuring the wrong thing or the half-open step is too generous. If closing sends full traffic at a service that's recovering, it re-trips immediately, which is oscillation by design. One probe request, close only on success, and a cool-down that grows on repeated trips.

The other common cause is a shared breaker over a heterogeneous dependency. If one endpoint of a provider is degraded and the rest are healthy, a provider-level breaker sees a middling error rate and hovers around the threshold. Splitting the breaker per endpoint or per operation class fixes it, at the cost of more state to manage — which is the usual granularity trade and worth naming rather than tuning thresholds indefinitely.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design failover for a platform where many agents share model access.

I'd centralise provider access behind a router that owns breakers, pinning and failover policy, so no agent implements it. Agents ask for a capability tier — planning, extraction, classification — and the router resolves that to a specific pinned model, with a declared fallback chain per tier.

Pinning is the part I'd be strict about. Every model reference is a pinned version, and version upgrades are a deliberate change that runs the eval suite, because a silent provider-side update is an untested deploy of the most important dependency in the system. Deprecation notices then become a scheduled migration rather than a surprise.

What I'd expose to agent teams is the quality delta per tier between primary and fallback, so a team can decide whether failover is acceptable for their use case or whether they'd rather queue. That's a product decision and it shouldn't be made globally — a background summariser and a customer-facing advisor have genuinely different answers.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We have a fallback model, so a provider outage is covered."

✅ Reality: Covered for availability, not for behaviour. A different model follows schemas differently and answers differently. Unless the fallback is in your eval suite with a known score, failover is an untested change deployed under pressure.

❌ Trap: "Retries handle transient failures, so a breaker is redundant."

✅ Reality: They solve opposite halves. Retries help when a fault is brief; a breaker exists for when it isn't, and stops retries from prolonging it. A system with retries and no breaker is a system that attacks its own failing dependencies.

❌ Trap: "Pin to latest so we always get the best model."

✅ Reality: That's automatic deployment of an untested change to your most behaviour-critical dependency. Pin the version, evaluate the upgrade deliberately, and treat deprecation notices as scheduled work.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • reliability engineering — the control set.

  • HLD reference index — circuit breaker and bulkhead in general form.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §8 Retries — the breaker is what stops retries against a dead dependency.

  • §8 Graceful degradation — an open breaker's behaviour is the degradation path.

  • §13 Version prompts, tools, model and graph together — pinning is that discipline applied here.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — a degraded model on a refund decision is a real risk.

  • §14 Internal agent platform — the router in the Tier 4 answer is that platform's core component.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Tests as the checkable signal an agent iterates against — SWE-bench (arXiv 2310.06770)

  • Deterministic checks before model-based judgement — Building Effective AI Agents (Anthropic)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • component vs end-to-end eval — the levels a check can operate at.

  • Reflexion & Self-Critique — the critic mechanism, when it's all you have.

What this note adds: placement and ordering. Gates are usually added uniformly after every step; the useful version puts them before irreversible actions and at the cheapest level that catches the failure, ordered so the expensive check never runs on input the cheap one rejects.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The order? Schema → deterministic check → execution → critic. Cheapest first.
The placement rule? Before irreversible actions, not after every step.
What makes a gate worth it? Its pass rate. 99% means it's latency, not safety.
Why critic last? Correlated with the generator; it catches least per unit cost.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Gates go before irreversible actions, not uniformly after every step — a gate on a read is latency for nothing. Within a gate I run checks cheapest-first: schema, then a deterministic domain check, then execution if one exists, and a critic model only if nothing above applies. The reason for the order is that each level costs an order of magnitude more than the last, so an expensive check should never run on input a cheap one would reject. The number that tells me a gate is earning its place is its pass rate — one passing 99% of the time is latency wearing a safety costume.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Schema check Always — it's nearly free. Nothing meaningful. Structured output anywhere.
Deterministic domain check A business rule can be evaluated in code. A lookup, sometimes a database hit. Limits, eligibility, referential integrity.
Execution check The output runs: code, SQL, a query. Verification time and a sandbox. Tests exist, or the query can be run read-only.
Critic model Nothing above applies and you need some signal. ~2× on that step, correlated with the generator. Free-text judgement output.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Schema Validation before execution. Negligible. Malformed rate is a model-drift signal.
Domain check A rules layer between validation and effect. A lookup per gated call. Rules and prompts can drift apart — version them together.
Execution A sandbox plus a retry loop on failure. Verification time; retries are productive. Iterations-to-pass is the quality signal.
Critic A second model call per gated step. ~2×, unverifiable gain. Needs its own eval to know it helps at all.

The redraw test: gates before irreversible actions appear as a check between the loop and the write lane — which is the same boundary as §2's authority decision, doing a second job.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Every step is gated and the agent takes three times as long for the same results."

Root cause. Gates had been added uniformly after every model call as a reliability initiative. Most steps were reads — retrieval, lookups, summarisation of fetched content — where the only available check was a schema validation that essentially never failed. The two steps that actually mattered, both writes, were gated the same way as the rest, so the gate that could have caught a bad refund amount was a schema check that confirmed the amount was a number.

Fix. Gates were removed from the read path entirely and replaced on the write path with a domain check — limits, eligibility, current state — that had a pass rate around 80% and caught real errors. Latency dropped and the gate caught more. The rule that came out of it: a gate's value is the product of what it catches and how often it fires, and uniform gating optimises for neither.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • component vs end-to-end eval — the levels a check can sit at.

  • Structured Output & Constrained Decoding — the schema layer.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §8 Fewer steps or more gates — this note is where the gate half gets placed.

  • §1 Is there a verifier — decides which levels are even available to you.

  • §4 Validate at the boundary — the same ordering, seen from the tool layer.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Coding agent — execution checks make this the easy case.

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — the domain check before a refund is the gate that matters.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Guardrails and human-intervention triggers as the designed fallback path — A practical guide to building agents (OpenAI, PDF)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • reliability engineering — degradation among the controls.

  • reliability problem — why partial success is the normal case.

What this note adds: the ladder, and the rule that makes degradation safe — a degraded answer must be labelled, because an unlabelled partial answer is indistinguishable from a complete one and is worse than a failure.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The ladder? Full agent → fixed workflow → partial answer → human → fail.
The safety rule? A degraded answer must say what's missing.
Why unlabelled partial is worst? It looks complete, so nobody checks.
Who can't read a caveat? A downstream system. For those, fail instead.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

When the agent can't complete, I'd rather it does less than fails outright — but only if the reduction is visible. The ladder runs from full agent down to a fixed workflow, then a partial answer, then a human, then failure. The rule that makes it safe is labelling: an answer that says "I checked three of five sources" is useful, while the same answer without the caveat looks complete and nobody verifies it. Where the consumer is another system rather than a person, that caveat can't be read, so failing is the honest choice.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Fall back to a fixed workflow The common case is enumerable; the agent handled the tail. Covers less; the tail cases now fail or escalate. A workflow already exists behind the agent.
Partial answer, labelled Some work completed and a person will read it. The reader must judge; needs clear labelling. Multi-source tasks where coverage is incremental.
Escalate to a human The output is consequential and partial isn't acceptable. Human minutes; a queue with an SLA. Judgement output, stakes high.
Fail cleanly The consumer is a system, or partial is meaningless. A visible failure the caller must handle. Automated downstream; all-or-nothing correctness.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Fixed workflow A second, simpler path plus routing to it. Cheaper than the agent — degradation saves money. Fall-through rate says how often the agent was needed.
Partial answer A completeness field in the output contract. Whatever was spent before stopping. Partial-answer rate is a quality signal, not just an error rate.
Escalate A confidence signal and a human queue. Cost moves to human minutes. Queue depth becomes the capacity limit.
Fail An error path the caller handles. Cheapest. Failure rate is honest and visible — which is its virtue.

The redraw test: degradation is a second path out of the agent, not an exception handler. If the diagram has one output arrow, every failure is a failure regardless of how much work got done.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "A compliance report went out missing two of its six sections and nobody noticed for a month."

Root cause. Two source systems were unavailable during the run. The agent's breakers opened correctly, it continued with what it could reach, and it produced a well-formatted report covering four sections — which was the designed degradation and arguably the right behaviour. What was missing was the label: the output contract had no completeness field, so the report looked like every other report. The reviewer had no way to know two sections were absent rather than empty, and the downstream archive treated it as final.

Fix. A completeness field in the output contract listing what was attempted, what succeeded, and what was skipped with the reason — rendered prominently rather than in a footer. For the automated consumer, a degraded run stopped being delivered at all and raised instead, because a system can't read a caveat. The principle: degradation is only graceful if the consumer can tell it happened.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • reliability engineering — degradation among the controls.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §8 Hard budgets — a cap trip lands on this ladder.

  • §8 Circuit breakers — an open breaker's behaviour is a rung of it.

  • §1 Is there a verifier — no verifier usually means the human rung.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — labelled partial coverage is the normal output.

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — escalation is the rung that matters.

notes.title: Optimising for the best run or for every run

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • pass^k — all k runs succeed — as the deployment-relevant metric — Measuring agent reliability (arXiv 2507.10995)

  • Benchmarks that report best-of-k, and what that hides — SWE-bench (arXiv 2310.06770)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Reliability Metrics — pass@k vs pass^k — the definitions and why they diverge.

  • agent benchmarks — what benchmarks measure.

What this note adds: what you build differently when the target is consistency. The metrics note defines the pair and Metrics before boxes chooses between them; this is the engineering consequence — variance is a design defect with specific causes, not noise to average over.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The user's experience? One run. Not the best of five.
The gap? p=0.9, k=5: pass@k ≈ 0.99, pass^k ≈ 0.59.
The three variance sources? Sampling temperature · unconstrained control flow · unordered tool results.
The cheapest fix? Bound the control flow. Variance follows path count.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Benchmarks report best-of-k and users get one run, so the number that matters is pass^k — all k runs succeeding. At 90% per run, five runs all succeeding is 59%, which is what "it's flaky" means quantitatively. Once consistency is the target, variance stops being noise and becomes a defect with three main causes: sampling randomness, control flow that can take many paths, and tool results arriving in a non-deterministic order. Bounding the control flow is usually the biggest lever, because variance grows with the number of paths the agent can take.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Optimise pass@1 Single-shot tasks where a retry is free and cheap. Says nothing about consistency. Users can just try again.
Optimise pass^k Production. Users notice variance more than failure. Brutal numbers early; forces structural fixes. "It worked yesterday" complaints.
Reduce temperature Cheap first move on generation steps. Less diversity; can hurt creative or exploratory tasks. Same input, different wording each run.
Bound the control flow Variance comes from path choice, not wording. Less adaptivity — the graph trade from §3. Step count varies widely on identical inputs.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
pass@1 Nothing. Cheapest to evaluate — one run per case. Variance invisible until users report it.
pass^k Usually forces gates and a bounded graph. Eval cost multiplies by k. You report a distribution; variance becomes an on-call signal.
Low temperature A config change on generation steps. None. Easy to measure — rerun and diff.
Bounded flow A graph with named transitions replacing a free loop. Bounds step count, so cost and latency too. Path distribution per input class is the new signal.

The redraw test: optimising for consistency tends to make the diagram more explicit — a bounded graph, named terminations, gates on the steps that vary. Variance and unbounded structure are the same problem seen from two angles.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Our benchmark score is 88% and pilot users call it unreliable."

Root cause. The eval ran each case once and averaged, so it measured pass@1 across a set rather than consistency on any case. In production the same question asked twice often took different paths — different retrieval, different tool order, different conclusions — because nothing constrained the trajectory. Users didn't experience 88% success; they experienced the same question answered differently on consecutive days, which reads as broken rather than as statistically acceptable.

Fix. pass^k at k=3 added to the eval, which came back near 55% and matched the complaints precisely. The remedies were structural rather than prompt-level: lower temperature on the planning step, a bounded graph replacing the free loop, and a deterministic ordering imposed on parallel tool results so identical inputs produced identical context. The score people quote didn't change much; the one users feel did.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Reliability Metrics — pass@k vs pass^k — the definitions.

  • agent benchmarks — what published scores mean.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §1 Metrics before boxes — this is the engineering consequence of committing to pass^k.

  • §3 Graph or free loop — bounding control flow is the main variance lever.

  • §12 Layered eval — measuring pass^k means running the set k times in CI.
